subject: Behavioral Economics
title: When Defaults Backfire
description: A quick win: understand When Defaults Backfire.

hook.text: Auto-enrolling employees in a 3% savings plan anchored them at 3%. Without auto-enrollment, many who chose to enroll.

buildup.text: Defaults set an implicit recommendation. People treat them as the 'right' amount, even when more is better.

discovery.text: Choi found that auto-enrollment at low rates actually reduced total savings for some groups versus no default at all.

twist.text: The fix: auto-escalation. Start at 3% but auto-raise contributions by 1% each year until reaching 10%.

climax.text: Defaults need calibration. Set them too low and they become ceilings. Set them too high and opt-outs spike.

punchline.text: A default is a recommendation. Make it a good one.

quiz.question: How can defaults backfire in retirement savings?
options: Low defaults anchor people, reducing savings versus active choice

details.summary: Defaults can backfire when they are set too aggressively, when they signal distrust, or when they provoke psychological reactance. If people feel manipulated by a default, they may reject both the default and the choice architect, producing worse outcomes than no nudge at all.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding when defaults backfire prevents well-intentioned nudges from producing the opposite of their intended effect. Too-aggressive defaults, poorly calibrated to the population, can undermine trust and trigger reactance that harms the.
takeaways: Aggressive defaults can provoke reactance where people reject the nudge out of principle
Defaults that feel manipulative erode trust in the institution setting them
The best defaults match what most people would choose with full deliberation

faq.question: What causes a default to backfire?
faq.answer: When the default is clearly not in the chooser's interest, when it feels manipulative, when it is combined with opt-out friction, or when the target population already distrusts the institution. Reactance makes people reject the option precisely because someone is pushing it.

faq.question: How can choice architects avoid default backfire?
faq.answer: Set defaults that genuinely serve the chooser's interests, not the institution's. Make opting out easy and friction-free. Be transparent about the default and why it was chosen. Test with the target population before scaling. Avoid defaults that feel coercive.
